explanations.answer: To deliver him from his enemies
explanations.explanation: David opens with “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God…” (Psalm 59:1). Saul, Israel's king, has sent men to watch his house, and David's first move is to talk to God. No speech, no scheme, just a prayer. I think that's a good order to do things in.

explanations.answer: To give him a sword to fight back
explanations.explanation: David never asks for a sword in this psalm. He asks God to deliver him and to protect him from those who rise against him (Psalm 59:1). Me, I'd have asked for a sword and then tripped over it on the way to the door. David hands the whole problem to God instead.

explanations.answer: To help him make peace with Saul
explanations.explanation: A peace meeting never comes up in David's prayer. He asks God to deliver him from his enemies and protect him from those who rise against him (Psalm 59:1). Saul is the king who sent the men to watch David's house in order to kill him. The prayer is about rescue, so that's where David's words go.

David says it plainly: “Fierce men conspire against me for no transgression or sin of my own, O LORD.” (Psalm 59:3). He says the same thing again in the next verse, “For no fault of my own…” (Psalm 59:4). That's two verses in a row where he tells God he's done nothing to deserve this. I think when your house is being watched, you say it twice.

This one is true. David says the fierce men conspire against him “…for no transgression or sin of my own, O LORD.” (Psalm 59:3). He's telling God that nothing he did brought this on. The next verse says it again, “For no fault of my own…” (Psalm 59:4).

David asks the LORD to “show no mercy to the wicked traitors.” (Psalm 59:5). That's a heavy line, and I think it comes from a man who is scared and hurting. And it's right there in the verse, plain as flour on an apron.

No trial shows up anywhere in this verse. David asks the LORD to rouse Himself to punish all the nations and to “show no mercy to the wicked traitors.” (Psalm 59:5). It's a hard thing to read, so I'll just say it's heavy. But that's what the verse says.

A second chance isn't what David asks for here. His words are “show no mercy to the wicked traitors.” (Psalm 59:5). Those are strong words, and I think they show how much danger David feels he's in. The verse is clear about what he asks.

The city is the word. David says his enemies return in the evening, “…snarling like dogs and prowling around the city.” (Psalm 59:6). Dogs on the loose in the middle of town is a scary picture, and that's the picture David paints. Verse 14 says it again.

David puts them in town, not out in the wilderness. The verse says they are “…prowling around the city.” (Psalm 59:6). Wilderness would sound like a nature documentary, and this is closer to home than that. The danger is right where people live.

The fields aren't in this verse. David says his enemies return in the evening, “…snarling like dogs and prowling around the city.” (Psalm 59:6). They're in the city, close to where people are. That's what makes the picture so tense.

explanations.answer: They think nobody can hear them
explanations.explanation: Their own words give them away: “For who can hear us?” (Psalm 59:7). They talk like nobody is listening. But one verse later, David says of the LORD, “But You, O LORD, laugh at them…” (Psalm 59:8). It's like trash-talking your boss in the break room while the boss stands right behind you.

explanations.answer: They think David will give up
explanations.explanation: Giving up never comes up in what the enemies say. The only words David quotes from them are “For who can hear us?” (Psalm 59:7). That's the sound of people talking like it's private. Sharp words, and a whole lot of confidence that nobody is listening.

explanations.answer: They think the king will reward them
explanations.explanation: A reward isn't what's on their lips in this verse. The words David quotes are “For who can hear us?” (Psalm 59:7). They talk like nobody can hear them. That's the thought that comes out with the sharp words.

David says the opposite. He says, “But You, O LORD, laugh at them; You scoff at all the nations.” (Psalm 59:8). The enemies have sharp words, but the LORD laughs at them. Nothing in the verse has Him afraid of anybody.

Right, the LORD isn't afraid of them. David says, “But You, O LORD, laugh at them; You scoff at all the nations.” (Psalm 59:8). The men were saying, “For who can hear us?” (Psalm 59:7), and now David says that God laughs at them. Nobody here scares Him.

David says, “I will keep watch for You, O my strength…” (Psalm 59:9). Saul's men are watching his house, and David turns around and watches for God. He gives his reason in the same verse: “…because You, O God, are my fortress.” I'd say that's a fine pick for who to watch for.

David doesn't mention family in this verse. He says, “I will keep watch for You, O my strength…” (Psalm 59:9). He's watching for God, and he calls Him his fortress in the same breath. The verse is about God.

No messenger shows up in David's words. He says, “I will keep watch for You, O my strength, because You, O God, are my fortress.” (Psalm 59:9). He's watching for God Himself. And I'd guess that's better than any messenger.
That's what David says: “God will let me stare down my foes.” (Psalm 59:10). It comes right after “My God of loving devotion will come to meet me…” So David is counting on God to come to him.

This one is true. David says, “My God of loving devotion will come to meet me; God will let me stare down my foes.” (Psalm 59:10). He talks like he's counting on it. And the verse says it's God who comes to meet him.

David gives his reason right in the verse: “Do not kill them, or my people will forget.” (Psalm 59:11). He doesn't want his people to forget. Then he asks God to “Scatter them by Your power…” instead. It's a strange prayer at first, but the reason is right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: So his enemies can turn back
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse talks about the enemies turning back. David's reason is “Do not kill them, or my people will forget.” (Psalm 59:11). What's on his mind is his people and their forgetting, not what happens to the enemies. Then he asks God to “Scatter them by Your power…”

explanations.answer: So he can show them mercy
explanations.explanation: Mercy isn't the reason David gives. He says, “Do not kill them, or my people will forget.” (Psalm 59:11). In verse 5 he asked God to “show no mercy to the wicked traitors.” So the reason here is that his people won't forget.

David asks, “…let them be trapped in their pride, in the curses and lies they utter.” (Psalm 59:12). Right before that, he mentions the sins of their mouths and the words of their lips. It lines up with the sharp words from verse 7. Pride and lies are the ones he names.

Fear and shame aren't in this verse. David asks for them to be trapped “…in their pride, in the curses and lies they utter.” (Psalm 59:12). It comes after he talks about the sins of their mouths and the words of their lips. So the trap is made out of their own words.

Greed and anger don't show up in this verse. What David asks is “…let them be trapped in their pride, in the curses and lies they utter.” (Psalm 59:12). It's all about their mouths and their words. Pride and lies are what the verse names.

explanations.answer: To the ends of the earth
explanations.explanation: David wants it known “…to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob.” (Psalm 59:13). That's a big wish for a man whose house is being watched. His eyes are on much more than his own street, and I think that's worth noticing.
David aims much wider than that. He wants it known “…to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob.” (Psalm 59:13). Israel is a small piece of that. The verse reaches the whole earth.

Jerusalem's walls are way too small for this wish. David says, “…so it may be known to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob.” (Psalm 59:13). He's not thinking about one city. The ends of the earth is how far he wants it known.

David says, “But I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning.” (Psalm 59:16). The enemies return in the evening, and David says he will sing in the morning. He sets a song right next to all that snarling. I think that's something to keep in your pocket.

Night isn't the word in this verse. David says he will proclaim God's loving devotion “…in the morning.” (Psalm 59:16). The enemies are the ones who return in the evening. So David's song comes in the morning.

The afternoon doesn't get a mention. David says, “But I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning.” (Psalm 59:16). The evening belongs to the snarling dogs, and the morning belongs to David's song.

David says it the other way around. He calls God “…my fortress, my refuge in times of trouble.” (Psalm 59:16). Times of trouble are exactly when he's leaning on God. The heading mentions Saul sending men to watch David's house in order to kill him, so trouble is in the picture.

That's right. David says, “For You are my fortress, my refuge in times of trouble.” (Psalm 59:16). He's saying God is his refuge when things are hard, not only when they're easy. And with Saul's men watching his house, things were hard.
